```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(cli.num_colors = 1)
set.seed(2026)
```

```{r setup}
library(nitRo)
```

## Analysing an expression

Pass code to `nitro()` unquoted, exactly as you would write it in a script.
Wrap several lines in `{ }`.

```{r}
nitro({
  total <- 0
  for (i in 1:length(values)) {
    total <- total + values[i]
  }
}, benchmark = FALSE)
```

Each line of the report shows the severity symbol, the rule id, the line
it was found on and a short message. `[fixed]` marks findings that nitRo
rewrote. Here only `BASE001` has an automatic fix. The running total is
reported, but rewriting it as `sum(values)` would change the structure of
the code, so that is left to you.

`benchmark = FALSE` is used because `values` does not exist, so the code
cannot be run.

## Explanations

`verbose = TRUE` adds an explanation and a reference to each finding.

```{r}
res <- nitro(if (class(fit) == "lm") summary(fit), benchmark = FALSE)
print(res, verbose = TRUE)
```

## Verifying and benchmarking a rewrite

When at least one fix is applied and `benchmark = TRUE` (the default),
`nitro()` runs the original and the optimised code. It first runs each once
and checks that the results are identical, then times both with
`microbenchmark`.

```{r}
m <- matrix(runif(250000), nrow = 500)

res <- nitro({
  row_totals <- apply(m, 1, sum)
  col_means  <- apply(m, 2, mean)
}, times = 20)
res
```

"Identical" means that the value of the last expression and every variable
the code creates are `identical()` in the two versions. The code runs in a
new environment each time, so `row_totals` and `col_means` are not created
in your workspace.

## Extracting results

```{r}
get_optimised(res)
get_findings(res)[, c("rule_id", "severity", "line", "auto_fix")]
res$speedup$speedup
summary(res)
```

## Analysing a script

`nitro_file()` reads an `.R` file. It keeps comments, reports line numbers
of the file, and never runs the code. The file itself is not changed.

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
writeLines(c(
  "# read and clean the data",
  "d <- read.csv(\"input.csv\")",
  "d$name <- gsub(\"-\", \" \", d$name)",
  "big <- length(which(d$value > 100))"
), path)

res <- nitro_file(path)
res
unlink(path)
```

To keep the optimised version, write it out yourself:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
writeLines(get_optimised(res), "script_optimised.R")
```

## Choosing which rules to check

```{r}
nitro({
  d <- read.csv("input.csv")
  if (d$flag == NA) d$flag <- FALSE
}, severities = "error_prone", benchmark = FALSE)
```

`categories` works the same way. Both arguments accept several values.

## The rules

```{r}
rules <- list_rules()
knitr::kable(rules[, c("id", "severity", "auto_fix", "message")])
```

Severity levels:

- **error_prone**: can give wrong results or errors in some cases.
- **warning**: measurably slower than an equivalent.
- **suggestion**: an alternative may be faster depending on the data.
- **style**: readability or robustness only.

## Limitations

Rules are regular expressions applied to the text of the code. They can
match text inside string literals, and most automatic fixes only recognise
the simplest form of a pattern, such as `apply(m, 1, sum)` where `m` is a
plain variable name. Suggestions do not know how large your data is, so
advice such as using `data.table::fread()` or running iterations in parallel
only pays off for large inputs or slow calls.
